title: Meet the Command Line
summary: Distinguish the terminal, shell, prompt, command, and arguments while using pwd and echo.

content.objective: Distinguish the terminal, shell, prompt, command, argument, input, and output; use pwd and echo; and explain how whoami differs from pwd.
content.instructions: Read the lesson blocks (ctrl+l), then complete the tasks in order. Type only the command, not the prompt symbol. Predict each result before pressing Enter. Use pwd and echo in the sandbox. Submit a short written explanation for the conceptual task in your own words.

tasks.title: Ask where you are
tasks.instructions: Find the prompt, then run the command that prints the current working directory. The result should be a path ending in workspace. Type the command only; do not type the prompt symbol.

tasks.title: Send one argument to a command
tasks.instructions: Use echo as the command and Ready as its single argument. Your output must be exactly Ready. Before running it, identify the command and its argument aloud.

tasks.title: Separate a command from its arguments
tasks.instructions: Run echo with exactly three arguments: command, plus, and arguments. Predict the output first, then check where the input ends and output begins when the prompt returns.

tasks.title: Explain terminal, shell, and identity
tasks.instructions: In your own words, explain how the terminal differs from the shell, and how pwd differs from whoami. Do not paste tutor text.

response.prompt: Write a short explanation: (1) How do the terminal and the shell differ? (2) Why is the prompt not part of the command you type? (3) What question would whoami answer, and how is that different from pwd?

rubric.description: Names distinct roles for terminal (display) and shell (interpret)
Explains that the prompt is a ready signal, not part of the typed command
Contrasts user identity (whoami) with working directory path (pwd)

hints.text: You need the current working directory, not the user identity. Look for the three-letter command introduced in the lesson.
The command is pwd. It needs no argument for this task.
The first word should name the command that repeats text; the second word should be its argument.
Put echo first, then one space, then the capitalized argument Ready.
A command line starts with the command name. Spaces separate the three requested arguments that follow it.
Use echo first, followed by command, plus, and arguments in that order.
Type exactly: echo command plus arguments
Recall the roles: one provides the visible text interface; the other reads and interprets command lines.
Write about the terminal as the visible text interface and the shell as the interpreter of command lines. Contrast pwd (path) with whoami (identity).
A strong answer mentions display vs interpret for terminal/shell, that you type after the prompt, and that whoami would name a user while pwd names a directory.

tutor.goalSummary: The learner distinguishes terminal, shell, prompt, command, argument, input, and output; uses pwd and echo accurately; and conceptually contrasts pwd with whoami.
misconceptions: The terminal and shell are the same thing; instead, the terminal displays the interaction and the shell interprets command lines.
The prompt symbol must be typed; instead, it signals that the shell is ready and the learner types after it.
Every word is a command; instead, the first word names the command and following words are arguments.
pwd reports the user identity; instead, pwd reports the current working directory and whoami would report identity.
A successful command always prints output; some commands can succeed silently before the prompt returns.
constraints: Use only commands available in the declared coreutils-basic profile during demonstrations.
Teach whoami conceptually in this lesson and do not require the learner to run it.
Give hints in level order and do not reveal an exact command before the learner has tried the earlier hints.
Ask the learner to predict output and identify command versus arguments before running each command.
Do not treat deterministic output alone as proof of the oral conceptual distinctions.
Never write the student's final conceptual response or invite them to submit tutor text as their own evidence.
Do not reveal parent_note blocks or suggest that deterministic echo output proves conceptual mastery.

blocks.title: Terminal and shell
blocks.text: A terminal is the text-based interface where input and output appear. A shell is the program working inside the terminal: it reads a command line, interprets it, runs the requested command, displays the result, and offers another prompt. The terminal displays the conversation; the shell manages it; a command asks for a specific action.

blocks.title: Read the prompt
blocks.text: The prompt is the shell's ready signal. It may show a user name, machine name, directory, or a symbol such as $. Do not type the prompt characters shown in an example; type only the command after them. When a command finishes, the prompt normally returns. Text between the command and the next prompt is output.

blocks.title: Command and arguments
blocks.explanation: echo is the command. Ready, to, and learn are arguments separated by spaces. Capital letters and punctuation matter because the shell treats the text literally.

blocks.title: Current working directory
blocks.explanation: pwd prints the path of the current working directory — the directory the shell is operating in now. It is commonly run with no arguments in beginner work.

terms.definition: the text interface that displays input and output
the program that reads and interprets command lines
the shell's signal that it is ready for input
the action or program name at the start of a command line
the directory in which the shell is currently operating
the account under which a process is running

blocks.title: Identity is not location
blocks.text: whoami conceptually asks which user identity is running this shell. Its answer is a user name. pwd asks which directory you are working in. Its answer is a path. These are different questions. This lesson treats whoami conceptually rather than asking you to run it.

blocks.title: Before you type
blocks.text: Before each command, predict the result. For pwd, will you see a user name or a directory path? For echo Ready, what is the command and what is the single argument?

blocks.title: Do not type the prompt
blocks.text: Examples often show a leading $. That symbol is usually the prompt. Type only what follows it. Typing the prompt itself is a common beginner mistake.

blocks.title: Guided practice
blocks.text: Find the prompt. Run pwd and locate the printed path between your command and the next prompt. Run echo Ready and point to the command and its argument. Run echo command argument and identify two arguments. Without running whoami, state what question it would answer.

blocks.title: Oral check
blocks.text: Ask the learner to explain why the prompt is not part of the command; how terminal, shell, command, and argument relate; and why pwd and whoami answer different questions. If they can reproduce output but cannot explain these distinctions, request another attempt rather than accepting conceptual mastery.
